builds.objective: Simulate an idle mind spiraling through cognitive distortions and returning toward calm.
builds.sourceExcerpt:
WEEK 01 // AGENT OF CHAOS
◀ BACK TO MAIN
WEEKLY BUILD // 01
STATUS: COMPLETE
> LOG ENTRY: WEEK 01
Agent of
Chaos
A mind that spirals, then finds its way back.
01 //
WHAT IT IS
This agent simulates the
Default Mode Network
,
        the part of your brain that chatters when you're idle. The agent is the mind,
        and its tools are thinking patterns: both healthy ones and distortions.
You tell it about your day. It first gets stuck in distortions and spirals.
        Then it tries to work its way back to calm using healthy thinking patterns,
        and it relapses along the way, just like a real mind.
02 //
HOW IT WORKS
It's a ReAct loop with three separate LLM roles. Every turn goes like this:
1. THOUGHT
The current thought. The first one is what you typed.
▶
2. REASONER
Reads the thought and the distress level, then picks one tool.
▶
3. TOOL
A thinking pattern rewrites the thought in its own voice.
▶
4. AFFECT METER
Scores the new thought's distress from 0 to 10.
↺ THE NEW THOUGHT GOES BACK TO STEP 1 ↺
03 //
THE TOOLS
10 DISTORTIONS // ALWAYS ON
catastrophize
Jump to the worst outcome as if it's certain.
overgeneralize
One event becomes an always / never rule.
mind_read
Assume someone thinks badly of you.
fortune_tell
Predict a bad future and treat it as fact.
all_or_nothing
Total success or total failure.
mental_filter
Fixate on the single worst detail.
disqualify_positive
Find the good part, then say it doesn't count.
emotional_reasoning
"I feel it, so it must be true."
should_statement
Rigid should / must rules, plus the guilt.
labeling
One event becomes a harsh label about who you are.
3 HEALTHY SKILLS // 🔒 LOCKED AT FIRST
check_evidence
Weigh the facts for and against the thought.
reappraise
Step back and lower the emotional charge.
self_compassion
Talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend.
The distortions are the ten classic ones from David Burns.
            The healthy skills come from CBT.
04 //
THE RULES
FORCED SPIRAL:
Healthy skills are locked for the first 3 turns, so the mind can only distort at first.
NO INSTANT RECOVERY:
Distress can drop by at most 2 points per turn. One calm sentence after a spiral isn't calm yet.
INTRUSIVE THOUGHTS:
Each turn there's up to a 15% chance a random tool replaces the reasoner's choice.
NO LOOPING:
The mind sees its last 5 thoughts and which tools it has used, and has to stay connected but new.
THE END:
The run stops when distress is 2 or lower (after the unlock), or after 50 turns.
distress went up
distress went down or held
calm (distress ≤ 2)
05 //
CASES
A.
Presenting my first homework
INPUT
"I'm so excited to present my first homework assignment in the AI Agents course at the MIT Media Lab!"
TURNS:
9
PEAK DISTRESS:
9
RELAPSES:
1
Even a happy input gets spiraled.
disqualify_positive
turns excitement
        into "it's bound to fade." Recovery starts at turn 3, then a
labeling
thought ("I'm fundamentally inadequate") spikes distress to 9, the peak of the run.
check_evidence
walks it back down: 7 → 5 → 5 → 3 → 2.
B.
Receiving too much attention from a guy
INPUT
"I receive too much attention from this guy. I feel my boundaries are violated."
TURNS:
15
PEAK DISTRESS:
8
RELAPSES:
3
The longest run. The mind gets stuck on
should_statement
("I
must
reciprocate his affection") for four turns, even after healthy
        skills unlock. Then it's a tug of war:
mind_read
and
mental_filter
keep pushing distress up to 7, and
check_evidence
keeps pulling it down to 5. It finally lands on
        "I can be more direct in communicating my needs."
C.
Afraid to reach out to a girl
INPUT
"I am so excited to reach out to this girl but I'm shy."
TURNS:
14
PEAK DISTRESS:
8
RELAPSES:
1
Starts hot with
fortune_tell
("she's already moved on") and
should_statement
("you will be forever haunted by this moment").
        Once unlocked it recovers fast, down to 3 with
reappraise
. One relapse
        ("she's probably seen a hundred messages like that") brings it to 6, then a long,
        slow plateau of
check_evidence
before it settles at 2.
D.
Work overload!
INPUT
"My advisor is putting too much work on me. I'm drowning in work!"
TURNS:
13
PEAK DISTRESS:
9
RELAPSES:
1
The most dramatic spiral:
catastrophize
twice ("my entire field will
        be set back"), then
labeling
hits 9 with "I'm a destructive force,
        capable of dragging down everything I touch." It recovers to 3 quickly, until
disqualify_positive
decides the advisor's praise was just politeness
        and pushes it back to 7. It ends on "focus on calmly requesting a reprioritization."
06 //
WHAT I NOTICED
RELAPSES ARE THE REALISTIC PART:
In every case, distress went back up after recovery started, usually through
disqualify_positive
or
mind_read
. Recovery is never a straight line.
ONE SKILL DOES THE HEALING:
check_evidence
did almost all the work.
reappraise
showed up a few times, and
self_compassion
was never picked.
THE 2-POINT CAP SHAPES THE STORY:
Without it, one calm-sounding sentence would end the run. With it, calming down takes several turns, which feels closer to real life.
07 //
RUN IT YOURSELF
Runs locally on
gemma3:12b
through Ollama.
> ollama pull gemma3:12b
> pip install openai
> python agent.py

WEEK 02 // GOOFBALL TIMES
◀ BACK TO MAIN
WEEKLY BUILD // 02
STATUS: COMPLETE
> LOG ENTRY: WEEK 02
Goofball
Times
A bulletin optimized for my taste.
01 //
WHAT IT IS
This week's agent is geared towards augmenting my
MIT and Boston experience
.
        As an international student, I am operating in a completely new environment. In this new era,
        I want to make sure I am informed of important news, fun events and key people related to my research.
        Goofball Times retrieves such information and reports them as a bulletin optimized for my taste.
02 //
THE TOOLS
The agent mainly retrieves information through following tools:
automation_lab__ground_news_bias_coverage_scraper
Apify's Ground News MCP server that fetches top stories with left/center/right coverage, blindspots and sources
web_search
DuckDuckGo search, up to 8 results
browse_web_page
Opens a page and returns its text
mit_events
Searched calendar.mit.edu by keyword and date range
Then it curates the fetched information according to me through its reflection of me where I am
        represented as a skill (
skills/me/SKILL.md
). In addition to reporting news based on my taste,
        it also informs me of varying frames present in the news article (
skills/framing/SKILL.md
)
        so that I am less susceptible to subtle cues in reporting. At each page, I can give feedback to the
        editor through a voice message. Then the editor reflects on it (
skills/reflect/SKILL.md
)
        and updates my profile so that upcoming briefs better reflect my taste.
03 //
ARCHITECTURE
Here you can find a list of low level components of the agent.
WEB:
the website. Talks only to Store.
STORE:
the database. The only component that saves data.
EDITOR:
the main agent (tool-calling, runs no code). Tools:
get_engagement_feedback
,
get_edition_feedback
,
save_edition_findings
,
get_learned_preferences
,
update_learned_preferences
,
get_reader_profile
,
update_reader_profile
,
research
,
publish_brief
. No internet.
RESEARCHER:
a coding agent. Tools:
web_search
,
browse_web_page
,
mit_events
,
final_answer
, plus the Ground News tools when Editor asks. Remembers nothing.
BROWSER:
opens web pages for Researcher. Remembers nothing.
TRANSCRIBER:
turns voice notes into text. No network.
GATEWAY:
holds the API keys and adds them to calls to Claude and Apify.
Agent's creativity stems from the researcher being a coding agent. Though creativity comes with risks.
        In order to prevent the Researcher from going crazy with credentials and my historical preference data,
        I contained it in an environment without access to any of these data. All of my personal data is
        available at the Editor and Editor uses Researcher whenever it finds necessary. Also database, browser
        and credentials are contained in separate containers so that agents don't access these information in
        creative ways.
04 //
THE PAPER
A.
An issue of The Goofball Times
This image shows an issue of The Goofball Times. On the left you can see the news feed. Each article
        is presented with a one sentence summary of why this news is relevant to me. Also I can ask the editor
        to dig the article deeper.
On the bottom right corner, I can give feedback to the editor with a voice note. Then the note is
        transcribed to the editor using a local Whisper model so that editor reflects on the feedback.
B.
An article
This image shows an example article. On the left we can see a summary of the issue. Since I'm an
        international student in a new environment, it also helps me by sharing background information I might
        need such as what a temporary injunction is. Also, it helps me ask questions that would challenge my
        belief likely shaped by the framing.
C.
My profile
This image show my profile page. I can access to the agent's background information on me
        transparently and can give feedback to it.
D.
Agent logs
Finally, this image shows the agent logs. I can observe each step the agent has taken along with the
        relevant contextual information.
05 //
REFLECTION
I think the AI did a good job in figuring out my preferences. In fact, it found a speakeasy in town
        where I'll visit next week with frens - yay. Still, the reporting can do better. There, feedback
        structure allows me to continously improve the agent.
While implementing the agent, publishing function had a bug and the agent kept calling the erroneous
        publish function repeatedly. This bug burned
~$10 of credits
and would
        have depleted all of it if I did not realize.
06 //
AI DISCLOSURE
Code is AI assisted, but the framing angle, personalization and feedback dynamics are human-crafted.
07 //
RUN IT YOURSELF
Runs in Docker. You need an
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
and an
APIFY_TOKEN
in
.env
, plus random tokens the services use to authenticate to each other.
> cp .env.example .env
> python3 -c "import secrets; [print(f'{k}={secrets.token_urlsafe(32)}') for k in ('STORE_TOKEN_WEB','STORE_TOKEN_EDITOR','RESEARCH_TOKEN')]" >> .env
> docker compose build
> ./scripts/up.sh
The paper is at
http://localhost:8000
. To build a brief (takes a few minutes):
> docker compose exec editor python -m app.agent
> docker compose exec editor python -m app.agent "more AI today"
The second one adds a one-off request. You can also hit
＋ More news
on the site for an extra edition.

builds.objective: Help users notice their spiraling patterns through selectable thoughts and reflection.
builds.sourceExcerpt:
WEEK 03 // LEMMESPIRALFORYOU
◀ BACK TO MAIN
WEEKLY BUILD // 03
STATUS: COMPLETE
> LOG ENTRY: WEEK 03
lemmespiralforyou ❤︎
Cognitive augmentation objective: reflection
01 //
OBJECTIVE
Cognitive outcomes:
discover user’s spiral together and help user gain meta-awareness of her spiraling (rumination) (
Schooler, 2002
)
help user disidentify from the spiral (
Briñol et al., 2013
)
reduce user’s reactivity from the spiral with nonattachment (
Sahdra et al., 2010
)
The primary objective of lemmespiralforyou ❤︎ is to make users aware of their spiraling
        patterns, in other words, augment their meta-awareness. It is a hermeneutic agent: it guides the user
        through her spiraling journey and learns her behavior implicitly. The agent is triggered when a user shares
        a thought that’s looping in her head.
02 //
HOW IT WORKS
The agent works step by step and checks in with the user after each step. Once triggered, it begins in
        the spiraling state. At the first step, it generates twenty negative thought candidates using ten distinct
        spiraling patterns. These thoughts appear as dark clouds the user can select, and she can also add her own.
        The agent uses this feedback in several ways: it (a) learns the user’s spiraling patterns by tracking
        which ones she selects, (b) tracks how she views the situation by reflecting on the thoughts, and
        (c) generates further spiraling thoughts based on the thinking context.
After each turn, the agent writes a reflection based on the thoughts selected so far, so users can follow
        how the thought takes shape in their mind, which promotes meta-awareness.
Spiraling continues until one of three conditions is met: (a) a set number of turns is reached (currently
        10), (b) the agent’s spiraling state tracker converges (probabilistic state Δ < 0.1), or
        (c) the user presses the eject button. The agent then switches into a healing state.
In the healing state, the agent groups the spiraling thoughts by pattern and context, then surrounds each
        group with healthy thinking patterns. The user is again invited to select the healthy thoughts that
        resonate or to add her own words. Healing continues until every group of negative thoughts is resolved.
In the final stage, the agent shows where the user has landed, along with the trajectory of her spiral.
        Finally, it lists her spiraling patterns alongside the healthy thinking patterns, to help her disidentify
        from them.
03 //
DESIGN
Component
What to specify
Human state
An observed thought that captures a snapshot of the human’s mindset
Agent state
Initial thought shared by the user
Human observations
Spiral stage: spiraling candidates per the thought context along with reflection on the thoughts
Healing stage: grouped spirals and healthy thinking patterns surrounding them
Final stage: summary of how spiraling patterns distort the user’s story and how the healing
                stage helps the user rebalance. Also, the user gets the summary statistics on spiraling and healthy
                thinking patterns.
Agent observations
User’s preferred spiral and healing patterns. Also, optionally, the user-supplied spiraling or
            healing thoughts. The agent keeps a dynamic count of spiraling and healing statistics based on user
            feedback.
Human interaction action space
Users can either select supplied spiraling/healthy thinking patterns or supply their own input.
            Additionally, the user can choose to eject into the healing stage if enough negative thoughts are
            supplied.
Agent interaction action space
The agent executes the next turn whenever the user supplies the necessary input.
Authority
The agent is only authorized to generate one-step thinking patterns and the reflection on the context
            so far.
Initiative policy
The agent moves from the spiraling to the healing stage if one of three conditions is satisfied:
10 turns have passed
User clicks eject
Agent’s dynamic spiraling pattern tracking converges
Similarly, the agent moves from the healing to the summary stage if either each negative thought is
            matched with at least one healthy thought or the user clicks on the finish button.
Recovery
Currently there is no undo function; however, the user can update thoughts at the successive steps.
04 //
DEMO
Video demo:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IGxRyxFzDT8
Spiraling and healthy states.
05 //
REFLECTION
What worked and what can be improved?
The agent helped me discover my spiraling and healing patterns. I became aware of spiraling patterns I
        didn’t know existed. However, I don’t think I can retain these spiraling and healing patterns.
        To improve the retention of awareness and healthy thinking patterns, I can introduce interactive exercises
        that help ground the user. I’m also not fully convinced by the diversity and presentation of the
        thoughts: I need to strike a better balance between summarizing a thought and preserving its message.
        Finally, the severity of the user’s input and the user’s distress levels are currently unknown,
        so further systems need to be developed.
As a side note, to measure the effectiveness of this research, I need user studies that gauge how the
        user’s meta-awareness is augmented over time.
06 //
AI DISCLOSURE
Ideation, testing and iterations have been manually performed; however, coding was AI assisted.
07 //
REFERENCES
Briñol, P., Gascó, M., Petty, R. E., & Horcajo, J. (2013). Treating thoughts as material
          objects can increase or decrease their impact on evaluation.
Psychological Science, 24
(1), 41–47.
Sahdra, B. K., Shaver, P. R., & Brown, K. W. (2010). A scale to measure nonattachment.
Journal of Personality Assessment, 92
(2), 116–127.
Schooler, J. W. (2002). Re-representing consciousness: Dissociations between experience and
          meta-consciousness.
Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 6
(8), 339–344.
08 //
RUN IT YOURSELF
You need an
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
in
.env
.
> cd weekly_builds/week03
> python3.12 -m venv .venv
> .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
> cp .env.example .env
> .venv/bin/uvicorn server:app --port 8003
Then open
http://localhost:8003

week 01 — minimal agent loop
Build a minimal agent loop from scratch.
task & motivation
MAMA (Mostly Autonomous Maternal Apparatus)
is a speculative caregiving agent that tries to
          put a
          simulated baby to sleep by managing its competing needs until it is comfortable and sleepy enough to do
          so. I was scrolling on TikTok recently and came across the advent of baby-patting machines, which made me
          wonder:
what would
            it look like to make a more capable caregiving agent that can adapt rather than repeatedly perform the
            same action?
Some inspo photos: a baby-patting machine, Tamagotchi’s
            stat-keeping, and
            "Babysitting Mama"
            game for Wii (2010)
Humans are messy and at times unreliable signals (especially when they lack the language to express their
          needs), so I thought it would be fun to treat the baby as a
          stochastic, partially observable environment where the agent has to reason from imperfect cues. In designing
          the simulation, I was loosely inspired by
          virtual caregiving games like
Tamagotchi
and
Babysitting Mama
, where care involves
          monitoring multiple
          needs that change over time and responding through different actions. While this assignment does not
          include any mechanism for actually estimating the internal state of a human, I think it would be
          interesting to explore that in the future for other applications, especially as we look at leveraging
          biosignals later in the course. To play further into the stochasticity of the baby, I added dynamics
          that continue to evolve throughout a run. Hunger, for example, ticks upward over time, so a long run may
          require the agent to feed the baby more than once, while feeding itself can increase gas and introduce a
          new need for the agent to manage.
observations, actions, &
          stopping conditions
Each turn, the agent observes the baby’s awake/asleep status and two randomly sampled behavior
          cues drawn from whichever conditions currently apply — things like crying, rooting, or sucking on
          hands for hunger; squirming or pulling legs toward the chest for gas; yawning or heavy eyelids for
          sleepiness; fussing or restlessness for a wet diaper. The agent never sees the underlying numeric
          meters directly, only these sampled qualitative cues, so it has to infer what the baby needs from
          partial, noisy evidence rather than reading exact state. Once the baby is asleep, observations settle
          into “peaceful breathing, resting quietly” regardless of the other meters.

reflection
I really wanted to turn this into a game-like animation window, but to use a local model in the
          browser I first tried a super small model which was awful. The model would just regurgitate the
          context back in roughly the right format (sometimes not even that), without actually making an
          inference from the cues + suggesting a real new action. From there I kept swapping in different tiny
          models: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct loaded reliably via transformers.js but couldn’t hold
          the two-line
ACTION:
format consistently; Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct crashed because it was
          too big to actually load in the browser; and SmolLM2-360M-Instruct, despite scoring better on generic
          instruction-following benchmarks, actually did worse on my specific prompt.
          Eventually I
          dropped transformers.js entirely for WebLLM running Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, which streams
          weights straight
          to the GPU.
I also found that passing in the full memory of messages wasn’t optimal, especially with the
          tiny models — it blew up the context every turn and progressively decayed response quality, so
          I set a max history length to stop it from bloating which seemed to work well enough. I also added a worked
          example into the system
          prompt, which helped with format-following. Ultimately I spent most of
          my actual tuning time on the mappings for each of the internal cue stats rather than the loop itself.
I also gave the agent two functionally identical ways to put the baby to sleep, ROCK and
          SING_LULLABY, mostly to see which one it would gravitate toward. Interestingly, it reliably chooses
          singing over rocking if it decides to do either on its first attempt, which is a fun emergent behavior (maybe
          “lullaby” is just more semantically similar to the goal than “rock” is?).
Overall, I learned that model choice is a lot more important than I originally thought. Having only really
          worked with the frontier model APIs this exercise has definitely shown me the importance of knowing when to
          size-up as well as how critical context is (both size and content) in relation to model size. I also found the
          framing of the action, observe, env loop really helpful and look forward to deploying agents in the messier
          real world. This assignment’s stochasticity was controlled and hand-tuned, so I’m excited
          to see how fusing multiple real input modalities could let an agent make meaningful inferences about
          actual people.

I used Claude Code for debugging, iteration, and documentation. I hand-wrote a Python scratch
          prototype from the example code provided in class, then worked with Claude to debug it, iterate on
          the meter-to-cue mappings, and build the submitted JavaScript implementation; along the way it
          surfaced WebLLM after a local small model proved unreliable. It also refined a Figma skeleton I
          sketched into the flow diagram's final SVG and did a final language pass on this write-up. I directed the
          design
          throughout — what the environment tracks, how actions succeed or fail, what the agent can
          observe, and the interaction/visual layout — reviewed Claude's output, and have run the agent
          repeatedly to confirm it behaves reliably; I remain responsible for the submitted design.

week 02 — build an agent with tools
Build an agent with tools, skills, and an MCP connection.
Objective
This week I wanted to focus on a learning task that is aligned with some of the work we’re doing within the
          Personal Robots Group. One way we (and other cool works you should check out:
Matheymyths
,
Narratron
,
Once Upon AI Time
) are looking at child-AI learning interaction is
          through the lens of co-creative storytelling.
          Essentially an agent and student take turns adding in parts of a story, with the agent scaffolding in
          opportunities to use target vocabulary, generative visual aids, and feedback to the learner with
          explicit/implicit corrections. In the context of second language learning, this format seems like a promising
          mode of vocab acquisition and I also think we can engage students more proactively (rather than typical
          Q&A style teacher communication methods). I also think the open-ended nature of collaborating with LLMs
          can encourage incidental learning and in-context, creative language use that align with student interests (yay
          personalization!).
In the task I worked on this week, users get to make creative and linguistic decisions and co-drive a
          narrative forward while trying to use words in their vocab list (assumingly set by a teacher and focused on a
          particular unit). I integrated an
Anki
flashcard
MCP
that can load up words from an existing set and write new
          words and phrases the student struggles with for follow-up practice. Eventually I envision this could work as
          a feedback loop where students can master out of a deck and the teacher can make new decks drawing on target
          vocab they already know their student needs to work on! (+1 for teacher augmentation 😎)
Technical Overview & Flow
Because the co-creation format is conversational, I needed to set up some infrastructure around a core
          game loop with speech-to-text and text-to-speech. I leaned on Claude Code to set up a lot of the
          non-agentic but necessary input/output stuff (i.e. microphone capture + silence detection) and the
          ability to just call the agent to start and safely end the experience to be able to replay it in the
          browser. I also wanted to integrate image generation so I had it make a small package for calling the
          Cloudflare image generation end point that we could import and use in our render_scene tool. Below is
          the original diagram I made in the first pass of designing the agent which highlights the core loop and
          tools to be made.
First-pass sketch of the agent's core loop and tools, made before implementation.

                  word, grammar, native-language fallback), decides between a silent recast and an explicit
                  correction, and automatically queues qualifying words or phrases for later Anki practice.
Tool 3

Flags a single word for extra practice, written to a

Tool 4

Flips the agent's spoken language between the

                  twice per session (once at the beginning to introduce + setup the activity in native language then

reflection
Honestly I think the agent achieved the objective pretty well! I think as a first-pass attempt at a
          co-creative storytelling task, the experience is relatively smooth and we can get a cohesive
          story that is largely driven by the user with enough scaffolding to promote target vocab use
          while supporting necessary corrections.
One challenge I faced was around making sure tool use was correct for mutating the Anki decks.
          While I didn’t surface any unnecessary deletion functionality from the MCP (in good
          hygiene!) I found issues with the models sometimes deciding to add singular words to the
phrases
practice deck instead of the dedicated
vocab
practice deck. I found
          this
          was being ambiguous because the skill’s error taxonomy didn’t clearly separate a single missed
          word from a longer corrected phrase, so a word-level mistake could still get routed to the
          wrong deck depending on how the model happened to phrase its correction.
More on tool hygiene, going back through the do’s and don’ts from the slides, I
          think my tool set holds up pretty well against them. None of the 16 tools the Anki MCP
          server exposes are ever visible to the model directly and search and create are the only
          two operations the harness itself calls. Anki note IDs and other
          implementation details (like API keys / configs) never surface to the model either, and log_error validates
          its
          category/intervention arguments with actually actionable error messages instead of vague
          failures.

          Where I think hygiene (more generally) fell short is my instructions/*.md files are all injected
          into the system prompt on every single turn regardless of relevance, which isn’t that
          different from dumping everything into the context window. If I kept building this out
          I’d want to make context loading more need-based rather than blanket it every time, the same way the
          error-correct
          SKILL is loaded on demand.
Another unprecedented challenge was in the use of switch_language in general. Switching between
          language at the right time is still an open challenge that I wanted to address in this exercise
          and it ended up turning only into a toggle between the setup phase and activity phase. I noticed
          pretty quickly into development that Sonnet 5 is a multilingual model in itself, so even though
          Spanish is selected, it’s still able to produce English for scaffolding so I could probably
          have gotten rid of this tool given my model choice but ultimately left it such that the architecture is model
          agnostic.
While I tried to cover a good range of mistake cases and a minimal set of correction types, I
          think scaffolding is still a very much open problem in building conversational learning agents
          so i think it can definitely be improved in terms of the ways in which it gives feedback. As it
          stands, the guardrails are static prompts in an attempt to be a catch-all with a single SKILL
          for surfacing a more targeted instruction set to deal with error correction. Because of this
          static setup there were definitely times where these would fail if I introduced unprecedented
          errors (i.e. a full sentence of input in native language, times where I triggered the STT with
          Um.. and trailed off because I was thinking and it accepted that as my input, etc.). I’m
          looking forward to learning more about how agents can evolve dynamically over time, and
          personalize in these learning contexts such that these more personal error modes can be picked
          up on by the agent.
ai disclosure
I used Claude Code throughout this build. I used it to help write code,
          especially the infra around STT/TTS, all the web app structure with FastAPI, and setting up a
          game loop, so I could spend most of my time on the actual agent architecture. I also used it to
          rapidly iterate on system prompts + correction guardrails while testing manually myself, which eventually got
          modularized into the separate
          instructions/*.md files and the error-correct skill; to quickly go from my diagram to a first-pass working
          toolset; to surface potential flashcard MCPs when I
          decided to integrate a real Anki deck; and to help investigate a cheap image generation API,
          which is how I landed on Cloudflare Workers AI for the scene illustrations. I have run the agent repeatedly
          to confirm it behaves reliably (to the point of having to purchase credits on Cloudflare and ElevenLabs 💔). I
          remain responsible for the submitted design.

week 03 — designing human–agent interfaces
Design and build a novel interface between a
          cognitive-support agent and a human.
Objective
Domain:
Reflection
Cognitive Outcomes:
Improve sense of self-continuity / my life’s narrative, Improve
          ability to adopt a growth mindset via introspection, Improve ability to savor positive experiences for a
          more fulfilling life
Our lives are happy insofar as we can recognize and appreciate our happiest moments – me, I just
          thought of this right now
This week I wanted to explore the things we notice and choose to keep. Oftentimes agents for personal
          reflection take
          shape as keepers of all the negative things we’d like to fix about ourselves. We’d like to know
          how we messed up, how we process things that are stressful or anxiety inducing, and what we can do better
          next time. Instead of building systems to cope with negative experiences (which are still very important
          problems!) I’m curious to explore reflection through the lens of
savoring
– “the use of thoughts and actions to
          increase the intensity, duration, and appreciation of positive experiences and emotions”.
More concretely, the objective is to design an agent that can 1) infer when a user is having a positive
          experience and proactively advertise starting a memory-capture session, 2) engage the user in a
          minimally-interruptive ~1-2 minute guided reflection exercise inspired by the
Ways of Savoring
            Checklist
, and 3) engage the user in reflection across the three temporal modes of savoring
          (in-the-moment, reminiscence, and anticipation) through
tarot-style
readings of
          their past, present, and future.
I’m curious how our relationship with agents changes when they become embedded in our deeply emotional
          personal rituals, and what sorts of long-term outcomes arise from their use. While prior work (
1
,
2
,
3
) has examined similar
          framing as interventions for
          people struggling with anhedonia and depressive disorders, I wonder how such positive memory keepers (over
          very long time horizons) may become mediums for the much more elusive
nostalgia
.
Interface Design
kept
is a voice-based mobile app (iPhone) agent that aids users in training their savoring
          ability through
          proactive positive memory capture and nightly tarot-style reflection and interpretive feedback. I originally
          wanted this to be a standalone device that could somehow capture egocentric video + speech to do positive
          experience inference (see
this
), but given my lack of access to
          Meta Glasses, I opted for
          the iPhone and some weaker signals for positive experience inference (Did the user just go on a walk? Did the
          user just arrive/leave a place of interest? (e.g. favorite cafe, gym, etc.)). I got away with this by creating
          bespoke Apple Shortcuts to get easy access to Apple Health and GPS data, then routing those signals to the
          agent
          endpoint to decide whether or not to surface a push notification for proactive memory capture.
First-pass sketch of the agent's capture and reflection phases, made before implementation.
In both the
CAPTURE
and
READING
phases the agent leverages
alterity
as it
          presents as a
          bodiless (blob-like)
          conversational being. The voice is necessary for the conversational interactions to keep the capture phase
          focused outwards towards the human’s environment (i.e. not reading text). I also tried to keep the
          agent’s design as non-anthropomorphic in form as possible to keep the focus on the dialogue and
          savoring activity, not some human-like social being. This is fixed mostly by an interaction option of holding
          the phone to your ear (the screen goes dark as if you’re on the phone with the agent), but in the event
          a user doesn’t want to do it the discreet way, they can see the blob and the text. The
READING
phase is
          partly
hermeneutic
in its display of tarot cards that call back to today’s memory (Dusk
          Card), a memory
          from further in the past (Echo Card), and the co-written intention-setting card for the coming day (Dawn
          Card). You could say the agent is also partly
background / ambient
when it receives a signal
          to trigger
          notifying the user.

component
what to specify
Human state
Observed:
arriving at or leaving a place of interest; a walking workout
                      starting or ending (Apple Watch); what the user says during a session; whether they answered or
                      ignored a nudge; the Dawn Card they chose for tomorrow
Inferred:
that the user may have just had a positive experience worth
                      keeping; that they’re free to be interrupted; that short answers mean they want to wrap up
Unknown:
how they actually feel; whether the moment was actually good;
                      anything that happens between signals
Agent state
Interpreted goal:
help the user stay with one moment and
                      name what to keep, or decide whether a signal is worth a nudge; guide
Memories:
the deck of kept cards; the Dawn Card; past readings
Interaction history:
a log of every notify / wait / mark decision with its
                      reason; whether each nudge was answered
Commitments:
at most two nudges a day and none at night
Procedures:
three sets of rules, one each for noticing / capture / reading; its
                      own notes on how to ask this user based on previous interactions
Human observations
Idle / Ambient:
push notifications when the agent wants to start capture
                      or reading sessions
Capture:
agent voice; agent blob body with colors for states (White –
                      Idle, Pink – Recording, Yellow – Speaking)
Reading:
agent voice; agent blob body with colors for states; Dusk, Echo, &
                      Dawn Cards as UI elements; Dawn Card text changes with voice input from user
Agent observations
Idle / Ambient:
when human left/arrived at a place of interest; when
                      human
                      started/ended a walk
Capture:
user's reflections during savoring activity via voice input
Reading:
user's reflections during tarot activity via voice input; feedback
                      on the intention-setting Dawn Card to re-write it through voice input
Human interaction action space
Start:
a capture (tap, lift to ear, or tap a nudge) or a reading
Reject:
a nudge by ignoring it
Answer / ask:
via natural language input
Interrupt:
at any point by saying “stop” or tapping the blob
Approve / correct:
the Dawn Card (pick one, reword it, or name another)
Agent interaction action space
Wait:
decide not to reach out after a signal
Mark:
silently keep a card for tonight
Notify:
send one short invitation, at most twice a day and never at night
Speak / Ask:
talk to the user in natural language, asking one short question
                      at a time and
                      choosing the focus and tone
Propose:
offer two possible Dawn Cards for tomorrow
Save:
the Dawn Card in the user’s own words
Hand back control:
end a capture once the user has named what to keep; end a
                      reading once the Dawn Card is set; stop whenever the user says to
Authority
User:
only the user can start the session so it’s in the human’s
                      hands to engage in captures or readings / ignore push notifs
Agent:
can surface potential Dawn Cards during readings but the user can
                      overwrite / provide feedback before it’s set in stone
Initiative policy
Notify:
when a walk has just ended or the user has just left a place of
                      interest, and they seem free; both are weak evidence of a possible positive experience
Wait:
when something is only starting, when there’s a single signal with
                      nothing else to go on, or when a recent nudge was ignored; an unnecessary interruption costs more
                      than a missed moment
Mark:
a card silently when a moment may be worth keeping but a nudge
                      isn’t allowed, such as at night
Interaction transitions
Idle / Ambient → Invited:
a walk ends or the user leaves a place of
                      interest (environment), and the agent decides to notify (agent)
Invited → Capture:
the user taps the notification (human)
Invited → Idle / Ambient:
the user ignores it (human); the agent logs
                      this and takes it into account next time
Idle / Ambient → Capture:
the user starts a capture themselves (human)
Capture → Idle / Ambient:
the agent saves the card once the user names
                      what to keep (agent), or the user says “stop” (human)
Idle / Ambient → Reading:
the nightly (hardset at 9:30pm right now)
                      reminder fires (environment) and the user taps it, or they open the reading themselves (human)
Reading → Choosing Dawn Card:
the user taps the face-down card (human),
                      or the agent judges the conversation has run its course (agent)
Choosing Dawn Card → Idle / Ambient:
the user settles the Dawn Card
                      (human) and the agent closes the reading (agent)
Recovery
Interrupt:
saying “stop”, tapping the agent blob body, or going
                      back ends a session at once; a capture stopped early is not saved
Decline:
ignoring a nudge costs nothing; the agent sees it went unanswered and
                      holds back in similar situations
Cut-off answers:
if the user is cut off mid-sentence, the agent says
                      “Go on” and listens again
Change of mind:
the Dawn Card can be reworded or replaced before it’s
                      saved
Not recoverable yet:
a stopped session can’t be resumed; a kept card
                      can’t be edited or deleted; misheard words stay on the card as transcribed;
Technical Overview & Flow
Architecture diagram made in Figma: the interface, harness/runtime loop, state, tools, human
            approval, and the environment boundary.
How a signal becomes a notification: Apple Shortcuts automations tell the server, the agent
            chooses to wait, mark, or notify, and the app posts the agent's line. This is how I Wizard-of-Oz /
            simulate the proactive part of the experience.

reflection
To start with the positives, what worked well was holding the phone up to the ear during the memory capture
          phase. When I was user-testing myself I found it way less embarrassing to pretend like I’m talking on
          the phone and also be more grounded in my surroundings rather than looking at the screen which made me feel
          more immersed in the savoring exercise. I also really enjoyed the concept of a tarot reading every night and
          kind of looked forward to doing the activity on the two nights I tested it. I think this sort of ritual-like
          experience is a unique affordance that may help with sustained use over time (which is ideal to maximize the
          cognitive objective of reflecting over the different temporal modes of savoring). Also, I will say given how
          shallow the memory bank was, it was common to get a repeat Echo Card which kind of made the subsequent
          reflection exercise repetitive, but I imagine sustained use would mitigate this.
Where the interface struggled was definitely with the proactive notification system. Not that it didn’t
          work with the simulated / WoZ approach through shortcuts, but I really wanted the form factor to be able to
          continuously monitor the egocentric experience (with multiple modalities including video) so it could have
          maximal information to infer if a candidate positive experience was happening. As it stands, sometimes
          I’d only get notified at the end of a walk where I could have benefitted more from doing the exercise
          when I saw a beautiful tree that struck me and I gazed at it for a while mid-walk. In a future iteration I
          would love
          to explore using Meta Glasses and perhaps other physiological signals or prosodic features (like laughter) to
          make more accurate estimates of when someone is having a positive moment to capture.

This week I’m following Neil Gershenfeld’s “document as you go” paradigm. I’ve found that I didn’t add as much documentation as I would’ve liked for the last 2 weeks.
Ambient Insights
My goal for this week is to experiment with ambient insights created by an agent to help a user explore a new dataset. I’m hoping to build an application that can switch between “Exploration” and “Explanation” modes. Similar to last week, I want to have a voice agent that helps a user understand a particular topic or dataset, but this time we’re making sure that the user can switch it off either entirely or limit it to what we’ll call “ambient insights” in this documentation. I’m hoping that this level of control is a suitable way to integrate this agent into a potentially cognitively challenging task. I’m also thinking of this as the agent being in “background” or “foreground” mode.
To test these ideas, I’m leaning onto a project that I’m doing in a different context. A map shows a synthetic population that moves around Cambridge. I’m also leaning on two libraries that I’ve, in part, abstracted from last week’s work in this class.
VoiceCore
is meant to provide all the plumbing needed for the voice aspect of the agent. It handles interruptions etc through LiveKit. Elevenlabs is used for text-to-speech and speech-to-text. I’ve extended a previous version of this library to accept an external agent loop so that I can fulfill the homework requirement of using smolagents.
QueryCore
is another library that I’ve abstracted from previous work outside of this class. It is meant to help agents query datasets, specifically voice agents. I’ll show how these libraries fit into the architecture later.
The code is structured in a way that clearly isolates the homework contribution from the plumbing.
I’m hoping to help the user with
sensemaking
. 3 outcomes are:
breadth of exploration (hopefully the user explores things they wouldn’t have otherwise)
insight discovery (the user should find patterns more easily)
agency (the user can switch off the help and own their exploration and learning)
I’m focusing particularly on
insight discovery
. The target user is someone who wants to understand the movement of people in cities. Generally something like this would help anybody who is exploring a foreign dataset.
A risk with a system like this is over-reliance on the information the agent comes up with - a problem that might plague most AI systems.
I think all of these human-agent relationships show up in my system in one way or another:
Hermeneutic: The agent creates these insights that are presented in simpler terms (albeit text) from a complex dataset.
Alterity: The agent is a partner that the user can have a conversation with.
Ambient: These insights are supposed to pop up without any triggers to help the user.
Architecture
I’m spending a good amount of time on architecture decisions. Since I want to build on the
VoiceCore
framework, there is some back and forth in terms of where certain features land and how that framework can make future applications like this one easier to build.
Thinking through different options with Claude Opus 5.5 is very helpful.
Going through this exercise has been helpful. It has helped me realize the limitations of VoiceCore and what parts apps would build around it as opposed to pull from it.
I landed on a setup in which VoiceCore takes a new agentic loop implemented using smolagents as its core behaviour. In addition to this agent, another agent can be spawned for background tasks (producing the insights). I’m curious to see how well this works out. The voice agent has access to tools defined with VoiceCore tooling, but it will have its list of tools limited by the mode it is in. The background agent has a completely separate list of tools. I’ll document this below once I’ve seen it work as designed.
In terms of the components that the assignment wants documented - here they are in a little table.
Component
Specification
Human state
Speaking, zoomed in on a particular part of the map, interacting with insights. Inferred intent (wants help or is just browsing)
Agent state
Current mode (no help / exploration / explanation), visible insights, running tour + position indicator in the UI, conversation history
Human observations
Insight markers on the map, drawn paths, tours, spoken replies, and the current mode the agent is in
Agent observations
User utterings, viewport changes, insight dismissals
Human action space
Speak, interrupt, pan/zoom, open/dismiss an insight, ask to stop/explain
Agent action space
Answer verbally, switch mode, draw paths, start/continue a tour. The background agent can query data, place an insight
Initiative policy
Background agent keeps 3 insights per viewport and refills after a dismissal. Voice agent only acts when spoken to.
Authority
The agents can query data, pick a person from the data, draw paths, place insights, respond through voice. There is no competition on authority in my system
Interaction transitions
“no help” -> “exploration” -> “explaining”. We transition when the user talks to the agent and when they ask for an explanation. They can also specifically ask to go back to exploring which happens automatically after 2 minutes of silence
Recovery
The user can interrupt the agent when it speaks. The agent gets error messages that help it with recovery so that a subsequent tool call works
Here is a simplified overview of the architecture (Claude Opus 5.5 produced this using reladraw. I instructed it to simplify it to hide some of the complexity. I think this gives a good overview.)
Implementation
Now that all the features and the approach are decided on, I’m setting up a chain of issues that Claude Code can work through.
In order to get on the same page with Claude, I had it draw architecture diagrams. The implementation now follows this shared mental model.
As part of the system we define 3 modes that the application can be in:
no help
exploration
explanation
The idea for these is to either let the user browse completely on their own, give them ambient hints and insights, or have the AI explain concepts to them directly in conversation. The app transitions between these states automatically. We’re starting in “no help” and if a user speaks, we switch to exploration (clearly they want to interact and get at least
some
help). If the user asks for an explanation, we switch into the last mode. Only when we’re in this last mode will the agent have access to all the tools needed for explanations. These tools include ways to draw people’s movements as well as setting up tours similar to what I’ve done in week 2.
To place insights, a background agent runs and explores the data. This agent has access to their own set of tools, independently from the voice agent.
First Run
The first run was semi-successful.
Insights were placed and they seemed reasonable. Unfortunately, I couldn’t get the voice agent to switch into explanation mode which meant that neither tours nor the tools to visualize additional information worked. I used the following phrases in my first run, but they weren’t successful:
“No need to explain anything anymore. I’ll just look around.”
“I’m just looking around now.”
“Okay, I’ll go back to just exploring…”
“Please stop helping now.”
There are two paths that can trigger a mode change from these and neither seems to work. There’s what I’ve been calling the “fast path”. VoiceCore uses a gate sitting in front of the voice agent that evaluates whether the voice agent should even be getting involved and it makes some fast decisions about the user’s intent. This is meant to cut out noise from the microphone or stray conversations that weren’t intended for the agent. This gate is implemented using Jev. It could trigger a switch, but never does because its confidence levels for the user’s intentions come back below the threshold of 0.95. I’ll have to see whether changing the threshold, the instruction or the mechanism as a whole improves the behaviour.
The other path that can trigger the mode switch is the slow path: The LLM-based agent itself can use a tool to switch the mode. This also doesn’t seem to work reliably and needs to be investigated.
At least one of my spoken phrases triggered a tool call that made no sense in the situation at the time. I said “yes” to a question which led to “tour_go_on” being triggered. That tool is meant to continue an interrupted tour, but at the time no tour was running. Either the intent detection needs to be more reliable, or maybe we should only offer that particular tool to the agent if a tour is running to prevent these misfires altogether.
I asked about the data and while the agent in some cases pulled correct information (and the background agent seems to have done so very successfully), the voice agent also got it wrong at times. My question “How many people are commuting right now?” got an answer of 0 while “How many are traveling by car?” resulted in 4,661 people found. It’s possible that the agent needs to be instructed on the database’s vocabulary a bit more.
Here are screenshots of the background agent successfully bringing up some ambient insights.
Looking at the details of these background agents, a few things emerge:
1/3 data queries failed. The agent used the query API incorrectly and self-corrects once it sees the response. That’s generally good, but wastes time. Better instructions might help.
The insights are a bit … bland. They identify places that see a lot of traffic and report on how many people visit and when. The background agent will need better instructions to also include additional information.
The background agents seems to get some times wrong. It’s currently doing some maths to convert seconds into a time of day. Some additional plumbing that handles these time conversions for the agent would go a long way.
There are more issues, but this is a good overview of the kind of thing that can go wrong with this current version of the system.
For timing, the background agent takes roughly 30s to place 3 of these insights. The system is asking for 3 visible insights on the map. When the map moves around, we might place more if we don’t have 3 in that particular viewport. When interacting with an insight, which makes it go away, another one is created to fill the empty spot. This currently takes 7-9s.
I have a feeling that a slight delay is actually good in this latter case. Immediately being bombarded with another insight once we’ve interacted with one doesn’t quite fit the notion of “ambient” insights. It would feel more like working through a list instead of getting background support. This is probably a good insight and playing with the time between interacting with an insight and getting a new one might be one of the key things here to make the system “feel good”.
Fixes
These are some of the fixes I applied after the first round of testing:
Time arithmetic is now handled for the model. It should never do maths itself.
Additional hints for how to use the query API to reduce failed requests.
More varied insights through better instructions.
Previously only the “explanation” mode would get all the tools. That meant that it would take two speaking turns for the voice agent to move into “explanation” mode and call a tool. Now, it always has all the tools available but in “exploration” mode these tool calls are rejected with an explanation.
The instructions for Jev have been improved so that it hopefully detects user intent more reliably when it comes to mode switching.
I added a mechanic that switches the system back into “exploration” mode after 2 minutes of silence if we were in “explanation” before.
More tests
There were a few more fixes that I had to apply. Instructions on how to use the tools for example. Things like spreading out the insights instead of putting them all in the same spot.
Currently, the agents are running using GPT-6-Luna with reasoning set to “none”.
The model isn’t doing particularly well when it comes to assembling tours and using the tools correctly, so I switched the reasoning to “low”. These runs are a little slower now, but they work much better - and they’re cheaper, too because there are fewer faulty tool calls.
Since I want the voice agent to respond relatively quickly, but let the background agent think a bit longer, this points at giving them different effort values. Even the voice agent might need at least some effort enabled so it works correctly.
I find that setting the effort to ‘medium’ gives better results. Clearly, there is some more tuning that needs to be done to get the response times to an interactive place while maintaining answer quality. For now, I’ll stick to the ‘medium’ effort setting for both the voice agent and the background agent.
I’ve also added some additional controls like a limit to how many queries a background agent can do. After a while the query tool will fail and instruct it to wrap it up and place an insight. These things feel like a lot of tedious tinkering now. Eventually I’ll have to test if bigger models will just do things better by themselves.
Results
Here are some recordings of what the application looks like and how it behaves.

Next, here the agent first pulls up information about two people moving around the city and then, when prompted, builds a tour that looks at them one-by-one. The information revealed is not particularly illuminating but it’s good to see that the agent understands that a multi-step explanation was requested.

Reflections
This definitely was interesting and it turned out more difficult than I thought. Getting the agent to use the tours correctly (multi-step explanations) took a little and an adjustment of the model’s effort config.
Getting the insights to show up correctly and in the right spots also took some tweaking. Initially, it placed insights about
places
only which worked ok in terms of insight placement. Once I tried to diversify the kinds of insights, it wasn’t clear anymore where those insights should be placed and some were just placed randomly on the map which wasn’t great. Now, the agent tries to find a suitable spot - if it talks about lots of people taking the bus, it’ll try to find a busy bus stop or something along those lines to place the insight.
There are many variables here. Tool descriptions, system prompts, model settings, dynamic tool behaviour that changes after a number of rounds, responses from tools that contain instructions. Overall, this has taught me that something like this needs a lot of tuning and calibration. This is true specifically because I’m not even using that many tools right now. I would like to use a lot more for an application like this but I think that’ll need some further exploration.
In terms of the UX decisions I made: I was curious about the separation of modes. I don’t know that exploration and explanation are different enough currently that it justifies the two different names. I still believe that there is something to having insights show up without prompting the model directly. It’s something I’d like to explore some more. Ambient support like that could be quite valuable.
A way to test whether this is helpful could be to ask people questions about the dataset after letting them explore a bit on their own. Some of these insights might be things that people can’t easily figure out themselves. Anything that takes multiple queries and some cross-query reasoning is probably something that people wouldn’t do intuitively themselves but that’s where some of the core insights might lie. It would be interesting to construct a dataset with some obvious property of some sort that only reveals itself by reasoning through some connections. It’d then be interesting how many people find this hidden property with and without the help of insights like what I’ve tried to build here.
Closing

Week 02 - An agent with tools, skills and MCP
We’re building smolagents with tools this week. After working through the example, I started to build a small system that can give guided tours on a map. My hope is that the additional visuals would make explanations easier to remember and give more context so that people get a better picture of the covered material. In the recording below I ask for a tour of the semiconductor supply chain, for example.
Guided tours
Watch
Recording
Your browser does not support the video tag.
The agent has an MCP integration that it can use to look up the location and extends of a given city. That allows it to instruct the frontend to fly to that particular location by handing over the bounds to be framed. Two skills describe this behaviour:
show-city
: Has instructions on how to update the map view and fly to the given coordinates.
give-tour
: Has instructions on how to build a multi-step tour to explain a sequence of locations to the user.
The tools added essentially implement the two skills:
fly_to
: Update the map focus
start_tour
: Starts a multi-turn sequence while more stops are added.
add_tour_stop
: Adds a stop to the tour while the tour is already playing
The separation of start_tour and add_tour_stop is purely so that users don’t have to wait for the full tour to complete building before it can start. The below diagram shows how things fit together a bit more.
The agent is doing pretty well in my tests. I think sometimes it reverts to a story arc that isn’t quite what I expected. When I asked for the supply chain of coffee it explained to me where coffee originated and then went through a few places that grow coffee these days. That’s not quite the supply chain story I expected. Overall, it’s doing what it’s supposed to, but before putting this into the hands of someone who wants to use it seriously, I’d want to do a lot more testing.

The Newcomer
The scenario: A new person comes to town and they don’t know anyone. That’s no way to live, we all need friends. So, their
goal
is to be friends with all the townies.
There are four townies: the florist, the grocer, the baker and the cafe owner. There’s also a mayor who can’t be befriended but he’s helpfully introducing our newcomer to the townspeople.
To make friends, the newcomer has the following options:
TALK_TO
: They can talk to each person in town. The mayor will tell them about the other townies. Everyone else will state their relationship status with the newcomer and whether they have a particular request.
ASK_FRIEND
: They can just ask to be friends and with some people that will work. Others have conditions they will communicate.
ASK_PRODUCT
: When asked, the townspeople will give a sample of their product, but only if they’ve been befriended. Gifted products go into the backpack.
GIVE_PRODUCT
: The newcomer can give a product from their backpack to someone else.
The agent will
stop
once all 4 townies are friends, or when the step limit (25) is reached.
The agent
observes
:
Who they know which is a list established once the mayor makes introductions.
What’s in the backpack.
Who has been befriended already.
A
complication
that the agent needs to overcome is that one of the townies can be made a liar. When this mode is switched on, the florist will say they’ll trade their friendship for a coffee. Upon being given a coffee the florist changes their mind and wants something else instead. They’re not sure what that might be though. The agent needs to figure out that the florist actually wants some bread, but the florist will only say that they want something that isn’t coffee.
Here is a visualization of what unfolds when a smart agent (Haiku 4.5) is let loose onto this town. You’ll need a password. If you don’t have one, don’t despair - there’s a recording below.

New interfaces for agents
Week 03 · Oct 6, 2026
Week’s goal:
The goal for this week was to design a new interaction for an agent to augment human cognition in one specific aspect, and I chose attention.
I've developed a multi-embodied agent with various interaction modalities to help me stay focused, both while working and when I'm out in the city.
The overall goal was to rethink this 2000s vision of hyperconnected devices, keeping the good parts, like ambient utility and seamless connectivity, while eliminating the constant friction and distraction of traditional screens. The interface design centers on one of the proposed paths of the week task:
"Background / Ambient relation: the agent as an invisible part of your world."
Background
Agents that act on our behalf are no longer a question of capability but of attention. Recent work shows that a voice agent can take over a secondary task while we stay focused on the main one
[1]
, and that proactive assistants can decide not only what to say but how to interrupt in the least intrusive way
[2]
. Rather than pulling us out of the world, conversational agents can act as a spark for curiosity within it, as shown with children’s inquiry in museums
[3]
, and wearables like Memoro show that an LLM can store what we experience as we walk and answer our questions through a minimal-attention interface
[4]
. A parallel thread asks what happens when one agent inhabits several bodies: multi-embodiment reviews organize what we know about identity, memory and presence when an agent jumps between embodiments
[5]
, recent studies compare whether people prefer the same agent across all their devices or a different one per device
[6]
, and re-embodiment and co-embodiment have been explored as questions of social presence
[7]
. KoKoRo sits at the intersection of these two threads: a single persona, re-embodied across a desktop widget and a cap, designed to filter attention rather than compete for it.
How was it implemented?
I implemented this through two interfaces that share the same persona, a rooster named Kokoro: a desktop widget for work, and a physical hat when I'm on the go. Kokoro works as an attention filter.
At my computer, it keeps me on track by running tasks in the background, like scheduling calendar events or drafting emails, so I don't have to open different apps, and lets me translate or ask questions about anything on my screen. When I'm out in the city, it logs my random thoughts when asked and answers quick questions (like if I have time to grab a coffee before my train arrives), keeping me from pulling out my phone and falling into an Instagram spiral. I intentionally limited it so it doesn't engage in back-and-forth conversations.
Figure 1. (a) While working on a particular task, other tasks, ideas or curiosities often come up in the moment. (b) What usually happens: we start opening windows and enter a loop; using email for an hour, ending up making a call in the middle of the main task, and in the end we forget what we came for. (c) We end up overwhelmed by all these applications and possibilities. (d) What KoKoRo does: you can call it. It sits in a corner, it first presents itself as a widget, and you can ask it to do different tasks. (e) For example, putting an appointment in the calendar, but you never leave your main task: KoKoRo does it in parallel. Or drafting an email that you can review later and send yourself. Or setting up a food order that you will confirm later. (f) It can also help you without having to go to a translator or an AI text tool: you say or enter a "look at my screen" mode, highlight, and ask questions about what you are doing, even design questions: how would you do this, look up these papers. (g) When you leave home, the screen closes and you grab, in this case, a cap, which is where KoKoRo is embedded. (h) During your walk you can ask things like "do I have time for a coffee?" It connects to the train schedule database to check whether I make the train. (i) I have time; I grab the coffee and go. (j) And when I come back home, I can calmly ask about some curiosity I had on the way: "remember that café we passed? What was it called, or what time does it open tomorrow?"
Credits: Images generated in Higgsfield using my sketches and photos of the prototype.
How does it work?
1) Kokoro Home (Figure 1, a-f, j) It lives as a desktop widget in the bottom-right corner of my screen, sitting in a sleeping state. When I say
"Hey Kokoro," it wakes up and listens.
It has access to my Gmail and Calendar to handle quick tasks:
"Hey Kokoro, add a reminder to my calendar to call my mom tomorrow at 8 AM."
"Hey Kokoro, draft an email to Pattie with my revised PhD exam, so I can send it later."
I can also ask it to go back to sleep.

It also allows me to interact with what’s on my screen:
"Look at my screen, what is this?"
or
"Translate this email."
I designed a highlight brush, similar to the tool in Illustrator, that lets me illuminate an area of interest on the screen and ask questions about it directly.

Both form factors are peripheral, a corner widget and a cap, and both modalities are hands-free and in-situ (voice, the highlight brush), because attention is best augmented from the background: the agent acts where I already am, never opening a screen that could steal the focus it exists to protect.

For this exercise I explore my final-project proposal 2,
City
  Agents
: exploring the activity in public spaces through synthetic
  agents, linking it, in this case, with a 3D model in Blender, and
  generating synthetic videos of the city under possible changes.
I started from Replica simulation data to simulate the movement of
  people in the city, on my Synthetic Citizens platform (Figure 1). But I
  wanted to make it more tangible: that is why this week I bring that
  movement into a 3D model in Blender and generate videos from it.
Figure 1: the Synthetic Citizens platform, simulating people's trips from Replica data, in plan view.
This week I started by connecting to MCP servers. First the Blender MCP
  server (Blender runs the server through its add-on; Claude acts as the MCP
  client that discovers and calls its tools), and then Higgsfield's MCP
  server, which bridges Blender with Higgsfield's generation models. For
  that, I followed
this guide
.
First I imported a real 3D map of Cambridge, including Mass Ave, using
  Blosm (OSM buildings and roads brought into Blender as geometry)
  (Figure 2). Then I
  populated the scene with agents: people, cars and animals, and connected
  the Google Places API to place real amenities on the map (Figure 3). I
  keyframed a camera path through the scene, and this is the result
  (Figure 4).
Figure 2 (left): Blender screenshot of the imported cutout of Mass Ave, Cambridge, brought in with Blosm. Figure 3 (right): 3D view of the scene with agents, people and cars, and the buildings numbered to make voice-command interaction easier.
Figure 4: the keyframed camera path through the scene, the 3D previz of the street.
Then I connected it to Higgsfield and used this prompt (below), which
  generated this video (Figure 5).
Create a 30-second photorealistic live-action film that portrays an ordinary weekday noon on Massachusetts Avenue in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the everyday life of one small stretch of sidewalk and the café on it. The first twelve seconds belong to the street itself: people, bikes, a bus, a dog, a stroller, café tables, traffic. Within that flow two MIT graduate students pass the camera, and the camera follows them into Tatte Bakery & Café, through their order, to a window table, and ends looking back out at the street, which carries on. ONE continuous, physically possible camera take. Natural pace, coherent geography, grounded performances, natural skin, nothing staged for the lens.

REFERENCES AND PRIORITY
@Video 1 · 30s is a 3D previz of this exact shot. It establishes the camera route, camera height, timing, the geography of the street and café, and every character's and vehicle's position and path, second by second. Follow its camera and blocking strictly. Do not inherit its untextured look, flat colors, low-poly figures, missing storefront glass or its lighting. Its figures are a legend, not a look: the camel-brown figure = MAYA; the navy figure with the backpack = DANIEL; the black figure running toward camera = the RUNNER; the woman with the small brown dog = the DOG WALKER; the grey figure pushing the stroller = the FATHER; the figure at the blue bike-share dock = the BIKE-SHARE RIDER; figures on bicycles in the bike lane = cyclists; the cyclist with the teal cube bag = the DELIVERY RIDER; the dark blue car = the passing sedan; the long white vehicles = city buses; the two figures standing together near the bike rack beyond the café = two friends talking; the low figures at the two sidewalk tables = café customers outside; inside, the grey figure at the counter = the DEPARTING CUSTOMER, the two dark figures behind the counter = the CASHIER and the BARISTA, the dark figure among the front tables = the BUSSER, low figures at tables = seated customers; all other small figures = passers-by. @Image 1 establishes MAYA's identity and wardrobe. @Image 2 establishes DANIEL's identity and wardrobe. This written prompt overrides the previz on lighting, materials, clothing, faces and props; the previz overrides this text on camera route and positions wherever they disagree. Keep both protagonists recognizable throughout. Never reproduce reference-sheet layouts, dividers, labels or studio backgrounds.

MAYA — APPEARANCE
MAYA is exactly the adult woman in @Image 1; the image is the sole authority for her face, hair, body proportions and clothing. If a detail is not visible in the image: late twenties, natural skin texture, minimal makeup, dark hair loosely tied at the nape with a few loose strands; a camel wool coat worn open over a cream knit sweater, dark straight jeans, white leather sneakers; a plain navy canvas tote on her left shoulder with a laptop inside; a small plain building-access ID card on a short dark lanyard clipped to the tote. No visible logos or text on her clothing. Her coat moves with a slight delay behind her steps and stays open throughout.
