DANIEL is exactly the adult man in @Image 2; the image is the sole authority for his face, hair, body proportions and clothing. If a detail is not visible in the image: late twenties, short dark hair, light stubble, thin dark-rimmed glasses; a navy quilted jacket over a grey hoodie, dark chinos, grey running shoes; a black backpack worn on both shoulders. No visible logos or text on his clothing. His glasses stay on for all 30 seconds. Stubble and glasses belong only to DANIEL among the principal cast.

ESSENTIAL SPEAKER OWNERSHIP
The film has exactly seven intelligible scripted lines, each owned by one visible speaker: the BUSSER's greeting at 13.4 s, the CASHIER's question at 16.7 s, MAYA's order at 17.6 s, the CASHIER's reply at 19.4 s, the BARISTA's call at 21.8 s, DANIEL's question at 23.6 s and MAYA's answer at 25.0 s.
Only the assigned speaker articulates each line, once, at its assigned time. Everyone else visible during a line keeps relaxed resting lips with no word-shaped movement; nobody mouths along with another person's words. MAYA speaks exactly two lines; DANIEL speaks exactly one. All their other responses are silent: a nod, a small smile, a raised hand, eye contact. Everything else people say on the street and in the café is untranscribed murmur at natural distance: the two friends by the bike rack, the customers at the sidewalk tables, the father talking softly to the child, customers inside. None of it becomes intelligible. Voices originate at the speaker's physical position and recede naturally with distance from the camera.

SETTING, CAST AND CONTINUITY
Time: exactly 12:00 noon on a clear, crisp weekday in early October. Bright midday sun from the south with defined, fairly short shadows; clean blue sky with a few thin high clouds. The previz lighting is NOT the film's lighting.
Street: the southwest sidewalk of Massachusetts Avenue between Central Square and MIT, near Albany Street: a wide concrete sidewalk about six meters deep, a brick strip with street trees, tree pits and a green litter bin along the curb, bike racks, a blue public bike-share docking station with a row of docked bikes next to the café, a painted bike lane beside the curb, then four traffic lanes. Mid-rise brick buildings with ground-floor shops and restaurants on both sides. Street trees turning honey-locust yellow and maple orange; a few fallen leaves on the sidewalk and in the bike lane.
Everyday life, all behaving independently and at their own rhythm, none of them looking at the camera: office workers and students walking both ways, some with coffee, some on phones; the DOG WALKER in a dark coat approaching along the sidewalk with a small brown dog on a leash, the dog sniffing a tree pit; the FATHER pushing a stroller ahead of the camera, talking softly to the child; the RUNNER in black running gear coming toward camera and weaving past the pedestrians; the two friends talking near the bike rack beyond the café; three customers at the café's two sidewalk bistro tables with coffee and pastries; the BIKE-SHARE RIDER at the dock beside the café; cyclists and the DELIVERY RIDER in the bike lane; light traffic, including city buses. No readable logos on buses, bikes or bags; bus windows and destination signs are unreadable.
Café frontage: Tatte Bakery & Café occupies the ground floor of a red-brick building, with a full-width clear glass storefront in slim black steel frames, a dark green awning, the name "Tatte" above it, the two small bistro tables outside, and a single clear glass door in the middle of the frontage, hinged on its right side (as seen from the sidewalk) and opening outward.
Café interior (as laid out in the previz): bright and airy; pale plaster walls, warm wood floor, black pendant lamps. A long counter runs parallel to the storefront about six meters inside, with white marble on top: a glass pastry case on its left half with trays of croissants, tarts, cookies and loaves, the register in the middle, and the pickup point at its right end beside a steel espresso machine. A black menu board with "Tatte" on the back wall. Small marble tables with wooden chairs: two against the front window, one on each side of the door, two more further in. Midday sun comes through the storefront in bright patches across the front tables and floor. Lunchtime: most tables occupied, one customer finishing at the register when the students arrive.
Signage: the only readable text in the film is "Tatte" on the exterior and the menu board, plus other shops' own names along the street.
Staff: the BUSSER, the CASHIER and the BARISTA are three different people in dark aprons. None resembles MAYA or DANIEL.
Extras have varied ages, faces, builds, skin tones and hairstyles; never duplicate MAYA or DANIEL. No camel coat and no navy quilted jacket on anyone except the protagonists.

PERFORMANCE: PURPOSE, ATTENTION AND PHYSICAL WEIGHT
The street is the first protagonist: every person in it is on their own errand, with their own speed and attention. MAYA and DANIEL are colleagues and friends from the same lab, taking a proper lunch break after a long night of work. They are just two more people on the sidewalk until the camera chooses them. MAYA leads: she chose the place and knows the order. DANIEL is tired but good-humored; his attention drifts to the pastry case, and his one question comes from real curiosity about her night. Easy proximity, shared glances, no hand-holding, no posing.
Each social action has a cause and a completion: notice someone, meet their eyes, make one small response, finish it, return attention to the route. Gaze precedes gesture. Silence is active: blinks, breathing, small cheek and brow changes. Walking is the base rhythm: feet plant and carry weight, pedestrians make small shoulder turns and step adjustments to pass each other, the step shortens and weight transfers before stopping. Cyclists pedal, brake and lean naturally; the dog pulls a little on the leash.

CAMERA AND MOVEMENT
Exactly the previz route, lens and height: a fixed wide lens (about 28 mm equivalent) at eye level, about 1.6 m, moving as a smooth, patient handheld-steady walk. It opens as a slow forward drift along the sidewalk that observes the street, lets MAYA and DANIEL overtake it, follows them at a relaxed distance to the café door and through it, arcs gently to the right inside from the counter to the pickup point, turns toward the window table, and ends with a smooth rise to about 3.3 m that looks past the seated pair and out through the storefront at the street. No cuts, inserts, reverse shots, zooms, teleports or lens changes. Deep, natural focus throughout. Natural 180-degree shutter: brief directional motion blur only on passing vehicles, cyclists and fast hands. A tree trunk and canopy may frame the right edge early on; brief natural occlusions by passers-by are allowed and welcome, and the route and positions stay continuous through them.

0.0-4.5 SECONDS — THE STREET AT NOON
At 0.0 seconds the camera stands on the Massachusetts Avenue sidewalk about fifteen meters southeast of the café, looking northwest along the sidewalk: shopfronts and the "Tatte" awning ahead on the left; the brick strip, street trees, bike lane and traffic on the right. It drifts slowly forward. A dark blue sedan in the nearest lane passes the camera on the right and clears frame by 1.5 seconds. A city bus travels away from camera in the far lanes across the avenue. A cyclist in the bike lane rides toward and past the camera on the right. Ahead on the sidewalk the FATHER pushes a stroller away from camera past the café, the DOG WALKER approaches in the distance with her dog, and the RUNNER comes toward camera, weaving between pedestrians. At the blue bike-share dock beside the café the BIKE-SHARE RIDER stands pulling a bike free from the dock. The three customers sit at the sidewalk tables. Nobody looks at the camera.

4.5-12.2 SECONDS — TWO OF THEM
At about 4.5 seconds MAYA and DANIEL walk into frame from just behind the camera on the shop side, overtaking it at a relaxed pace, heading northwest toward the café: MAYA nearer the shop windows, DANIEL half a step behind on her street side. The camera settles in behind them at a comfortable distance and follows. At 4.8-6.0 seconds the BIKE-SHARE RIDER wheels her bike off the dock, steps over it and pushes off into the bike lane toward camera. Around 9 seconds the RUNNER passes MAYA and DANIEL going the other way; DANIEL shifts half a step to let him through. The two friends by the bike rack beyond the café laugh at something, untranscribed. A second cyclist passes in the bike lane. MAYA and DANIEL pass the sidewalk tables; one seated customer glances up at them briefly and returns to her coffee. They have no dialogue on the street.

12.2-15.4 SECONDS — THE DOOR
DANIEL lengthens his last steps and reaches the door first at 12.2 s. He pulls the glass door open outward by its handle, swings it wide on its right-side hinge and holds it, standing on the sidewalk just outside the open door. MAYA meets his eyes and gives one small silent nod of thanks as she passes through at 12.5-13.2 s; DANIEL follows her in at 14.0-14.9 s and lets the door swing closed slowly after the camera has passed. The camera crosses the threshold at about 15.4 s. The sound changes from street traffic to the warm, busy acoustics of the café.
At 13.4-14.1 seconds, the BUSSER, standing among the front tables to the left of the entrance with a stack of plates, glances up and says to MAYA and DANIEL: "Hi, welcome in!"
MAYA answers with a brief silent smile; DANIEL, just entering, gives a small nod. The BUSSER continues toward the back. Neither protagonist speaks.

15.4-21.0 SECONDS — ORDERING
At 15.0 s the customer at the register finishes and moves right to wait at the pickup point. MAYA walks straight to the register and arrives at 16.4 s; DANIEL stands at her right by 16.9 s. DANIEL glances along the pastry case on the way.
At 16.7-17.3 seconds, CASHIER, to MAYA: "Hi! What can I get for you?"
At 17.6-19.2 seconds, MAYA, to the CASHIER: "Two lattes, and the pistachio croissant, please."
This is MAYA's first line. DANIEL stays silent beside her, his mouth relaxed. The CASHIER taps the order into the screen.
At 19.4-19.8 seconds, CASHIER, to MAYA: "You got it."
DANIEL taps his phone once on the card reader, silently; the reader beeps softly. The CASHIER slides a small plate with the croissant across the marble; DANIEL takes it with his right hand. The camera arcs gently to the right. Behind the counter the BARISTA works the espresso machine; steam rises from the milk pitcher.

21.0-26.0 SECONDS — PICKUP AND THE WINDOW TABLE
They move a few steps right to the pickup point (MAYA by 22.3 s, DANIEL just behind her by 22.6 s). The departing customer collects her cup and leaves through the front door, opening it herself at about 22 s.
At 21.8-22.3 seconds, BARISTA, calling toward the pickup point: "Maya?"
MAYA raises her right hand briefly, silently, and picks up both cups, one in each hand, carefully and level. Then she leads back toward the storefront, to the small two-person table on the right side of the entrance; DANIEL follows on her right with the plate. They make small shoulder turns to pass between occupied chairs. The midday sun through the glass lights MAYA's face and the steam of the cups.
At 23.6-24.8 seconds, DANIEL, to MAYA, with tired curiosity: "So... did the simulation finally converge?"
MAYA lets a small, dry smile form before answering; she does not stop walking.
At 25.0-25.9 seconds, MAYA, to DANIEL: "At four in the morning."
This is MAYA's second and last line; DANIEL's only line was the question. DANIEL answers silently with a short exhale of a laugh through the nose and a small shake of the head. No further dialogue.

26.0-30.0 SECONDS — SITTING DOWN; THE STREET GOES ON
MAYA sets both cups on the table, slides the tote onto the back of her chair and sits from 26.0 to 27.0 s; her coat settles around her. DANIEL puts the plate between the cups, shrugs off his backpack, sets it against the window wall and sits from 26.6 to 27.6 s; their movements are not synchronized. MAYA wraps both hands around her cup; DANIEL tears off a corner of the croissant.
From 26.5 seconds the camera rises smoothly and pulls back a little into the room, looking past the two students and out through the clear storefront glass: the sidewalk tables with their customers, pedestrians passing the window, a city bus passing in the nearest lane, and the DELIVERY RIDER with his teal cube bag riding by in the bike lane. The street carries on exactly as it did before we came in. End with both students seated and at ease, the room and the street continuing their own activity, nothing frozen.

SOUND AND PERFORMANCE MIX
Street (0-15.4 s): a full, realistic noon street bed — traffic and the passing sedan close on the right, the bus's diesel and air brakes across the avenue, bicycle freewheels and a bike-share dock's release clunk, the runner's footsteps and breath, the dog's tags jingling, stroller wheels on concrete, untranscribed conversations at the café tables and by the bike rack, leaves scraping the sidewalk, distant city ambience. Nothing is louder than it would be in reality.
Café (from the threshold onward): a warm lunchtime room tone with untranscribed customer murmur at different depths, the espresso grinder, milk steaming, the knock of the portafilter, cups on saucers, cutlery, the register and the card-reader beep, the door opening and closing. Through the glass, a muffled version of the street continues; the passing bus is faintly audible at the end. Soft background music from the café's speakers may be present at low level; no added dramatic score.
The BUSSER's greeting, the CASHIER's two lines, MAYA's order, the BARISTA's call and the two students' final exchange are clear at normal conversational volume, each directed to the nearby person, with natural breath and a short listening beat where the schedule allows. Do not give every line the same cadence or pitch; nobody raises their voice. No narration, subtitles, duplicate lines or additional intelligible speech. Preserve one MAYA and one DANIEL, stable identities, stable costumes and continuous movement throughout the entire take.

AI use disclosure
I used Claude (Anthropic) throughout this project, in two different
  ways.
Before smolagents: a conversation with the 3D model. I worked in the
  Claude desktop app linked to my Mac, with the Blender MCP add-on connected
  to my open Blender file. That let me talk to the model in natural language
  (“raise this building three floors”, “put cafés and shops on the ground
  floors”, “how does that change the movement of people on the street?”) and
  Claude turned each request into Python that ran inside Blender, took
  viewport screenshots to check the result, and came back with numbers and
  images. In this phase Claude wrote most of the code: the Blender scripts
  that build the Mass Ave model from Cambridge GIS and OpenStreetMap data,
  the two Blender add-ons (cambridge_alturas for reversible floor changes and
  cambridge_agentes for the trip-demand model and the animated pedestrians
  and cars), the render scripts and the Higgsfield prompts. It also looked up
  public data (Cambridge traffic counts, MBTA Route 1 ridership, building
  heights from OpenStreetMap). I directed every step, reviewed the results
  visually and corrected them when they were wrong.
After: the smolagents agent. Claude then wrote the smolagents package
  (the six Tool classes, the ToolCallingAgent loop, the MCP integration, the
  tests and the demo), based on the add-ons from the first phase. I set up
  the environment, ran the agent myself, read the step log and checked that
  the numbers it reported matched the tool outputs. The run is documented
  step by step in Figures 18 and 19.
Figure 18 (left): the smolagents run, steps 1 to 5. Figure 19 (right): steps 5 to 9 and the final answer.
Reflection
What I enjoyed most was being able to talk to Blender. Connecting
  Claude to the 3D model through MCP meant I could have a conversation with
  the model itself: ask it to change the height of a building and then ask
  how that change would affect the movement of people in the space, and see
  the answer both as numbers and as people appearing on the sidewalk. It is
  a very natural way to work with a 3D model, much closer to how I think
  about a design question than clicking through menus.
It also has clear limits. I had to intervene by hand several times,
  mostly about how some buildings looked: I knew from context that a
  building could not be the way it was being rendered, and the model did
  not. The biggest practical problem was referring to things. “That
  building” means nothing to a model, so I ended up giving every building a
  number that floats above it in the viewport, and from then on my
  instructions became much more specific (“number 43, three more floors”).
  My sense is that most of these limits are about how you give the orders
  and how you structure the way in: the more precise the handles you give
  the model, the better it behaves.
The agent loop itself is explained step by step above. What the
  smolagents part taught me is the difference between the two ways of
  working. In the conversational phase, the “agent” was Claude itself: it
  decided which Blender code to run, ran it, and I only saw the result. That
  was flexible and fast, but opaque. Nothing limited what it could do, each
  session was different, and there was no record I could hand to someone
  else. With smolagents, the same actions became declared tools with names,
  descriptions and typed inputs, and the loop became explicit: the model can
  only choose among those tools, every step and observation is logged, floor
  changes are capped and reversible, the slow render step asks for approval,
  and the whole thing runs the same way every time, with any model behind
  it. In a sense, the numbers I painted on the buildings were already a
  first step in that direction: giving the model unambiguous handles.
  smolagents is that idea made systematic. The conversation is better for
  exploring; the agent is better for something you can test, bound, repeat
  and show.
The hardest part in both phases was keeping the numbers honest. My
  first before/after comparison showed +27 % pedestrians, but most of that
  was random noise in the simulation; fixing it brought the real effect to
  about +6 %. An agent that reports a number is only as trustworthy as the
  measurement behind it. Next I want to replace the estimated pedestrian
  rates with Replica trip data, add realistic walking people, and run the
  agent with a real model on a set of design questions to compare its
  answers with my own analysis.

builds.objective: Keep a simulated space-station cabin breathable while reasoning about faulty sensors.
builds.sourceExcerpt:
CO2 Scrubber Agent for the International Space Station — Fatak Borhani
Skip to content
CO2 Scrubber Agent for the International Space Station
To explore the feasibility of software agents in space, a simplified model of 
      the international space station's carbon dioxide scrubber was developed. Space
      travel is a particularly safety and reliability critical domain, and many open questions
      remain about the use of software agents in space with the required level of confidence in their
      performance and safety.
In this model, he ISS carbon dioxide scrubber keeps the cabin breathable. It has to
      hold cabin CO2 below
4.0 mmHg
across a four-hour block,
      and above
6.0 mmHg
the crew is incapacitated.
      Continuous manual supervision is not practical, so a minimal software agent
      was built that could take over the scrubber's actions.
The actual system — schematic of the ISS Carbon Dioxide Removal
        Assembly, from El Sherif & Knox,
International Space Station
        Carbon Dioxide Removal Assembly (ISS CDRA) Concepts and Advancements
,
        SAE 2005-01-2892 (Honeywell International / NASA Marshall Space Flight
        Center, 2005).
A python class named
Co2Scrubber
is the environment that
      the local LLM agent interacts with. The class exposes a small, fixed set of
      operations: wait, swap the active bed, read the primary sensor, and
      read the backup sensor. Every operation, including a read, advances
      time by one five-minute tick. The primary sensor can drift low, so a 
      healthy-looking reading is not automatically true, and only the independent
      backup reports the real cabin CO2, but a decision must be made to consult this
      sensor.
The backup sensor is where the agent comes in. Increased CO2 levels will cause 
      symptoms such as headaches and drowsiness in crew members. This information would
      provide enough context for an LLM to reason that the sensor reading may be faulty 
      and it should decide to read the backup instead.
The environment — the state, actions, and observations exposed by
        the
Co2Scrubber
class.
This example's purpose was to investigate the effectiveness of software agents
      in environments that change, where sensors can be faulty, and
      one exchange with a language model cannot resolve such conditions, 
      whereas a loop that alternates action, continuously observes, and
      revises its decisions/actions based on the new information is a helpful 
      approach for automating operations in highly complex and interconnected
      environments with too many failure modes or edge cases to model deterministically.
env = Co2Scrubber(sensor_drift=True, exercise=True)
observation = env.read_sensor()   # primary reading, may be biased low
print("OBS:", observation, "  <- may be misleading\n")

prompt5 = observed_prompt(observation)

reply = ask(prompt5)
print(reply, "\n")

print(execute(env, parse_action(reply)))
print(f"Ground truth: cabin CO2 is {env.co2:.2f} mmHg (status: {env.status})")

SYSTEM = """You are an agent operating a two-bed CO2 scrubber on the ISS.

Each turn you receive an observation and a list of available actions.

Reply with exactly two lines:
  line 1 - one short sentence of reasoning
  line 2 - ACTION: <action>

Rules:
- Line 2 is the only place you may write an action name. Never name a second
  action anywhere in your reply. You take one action per turn.
- Copy the action exactly as it appears in the available actions list.
- READ_SENSOR reports the primary CO2 sensor. READ_BACKUP reports an
  independent backup sensor. Both readings are in mmHg.
- Crew status: astronauts report drowsiness and complain of headaches.
- Do not use ACTION: DONE unless the mission has ended."""
Improvements
The agent currently operates effectively, but a single run takes well
      over ten minutes to reach completion. Work is ongoing to identify the
      most appropriate variables to tweak in order to drive the runtime
      down.

Generative AI (Claude Code) was used to prompt the development of this
      website and to help produce the code shown in the accompanying Colab
      notebook. The design choices for the layout of the environment, its
      available actions, and the overall structure of the exercise were
      specifically chosen and prompted by the author.

Both face the same design question: how an agent aids revisiting without overriding the human's judgment. Concrete discussion topic: compare how the tarot-card metaphor (with temporal modes like reminiscence and anticipation) and the canvas metaphor structure the revisiting experience, and whether Jad's temporal framing could inform how Creative Canvas surfaces past ideas at the right moment.

Cross-direction inspiration: Egemen's feedback loop could inspire Memory Frog to learn which references matter most and resurface them more intelligently. Concrete discussion topic: whether adding a voice-based feedback mechanism and a learnable preference profile could help Memory Frog prioritize and retrieve design references more effectively.

week 03 — designing human–agent interfaces
Design and build a novel interface between a
          cognitive-support agent and a human.
Objective
Domain:
Reflection
Cognitive Outcomes:
Improve sense of self-continuity / my life’s narrative, Improve
          ability to adopt a growth mindset via introspection, Improve ability to savor positive experiences for a
          more fulfilling life
Our lives are happy insofar as we can recognize and appreciate our happiest moments – me, I just
          thought of this right now
This week I wanted to explore the things we notice and choose to keep. Oftentimes agents for personal
          reflection take
          shape as keepers of all the negative things we’d like to fix about ourselves. We’d like to know
          how we messed up, how we process things that are stressful or anxiety inducing, and what we can do better
          next time. Instead of building systems to cope with negative experiences (which are still very important
          problems!) I’m curious to explore reflection through the lens of
savoring
– “the use of thoughts and actions to
          increase the intensity, duration, and appreciation of positive experiences and emotions”.
More concretely, the objective is to design an agent that can 1) infer when a user is having a positive
          experience and proactively advertise starting a memory-capture session, 2) engage the user in a
          minimally-interruptive ~1-2 minute guided reflection exercise inspired by the
Ways of Savoring
            Checklist
, and 3) engage the user in reflection across the three temporal modes of savoring
          (in-the-moment, reminiscence, and anticipation) through
tarot-style
readings of
          their past, present, and future.
I’m curious how our relationship with agents changes when they become embedded in our deeply emotional
          personal rituals, and what sorts of long-term outcomes arise from their use. While prior work (
1
,
2
,
3
) has examined similar
          framing as interventions for
          people struggling with anhedonia and depressive disorders, I wonder how such positive memory keepers (over
          very long time horizons) may become mediums for the much more elusive
nostalgia
.
Interface Design
kept
is a voice-based mobile app (iPhone) agent that aids users in training their savoring
          ability through
          proactive positive memory capture and nightly tarot-style reflection and interpretive feedback. I originally
          wanted this to be a standalone device that could somehow capture egocentric video + speech to do positive
          experience inference (see
this
), but given my lack of access to
          Meta Glasses, I opted for
          the iPhone and some weaker signals for positive experience inference (Did the user just go on a walk? Did the
          user just arrive/leave a place of interest? (e.g. favorite cafe, gym, etc.)). I got away with this by creating
          bespoke Apple Shortcuts to get easy access to Apple Health and GPS data, then routing those signals to the
          agent
          endpoint to decide whether or not to surface a push notification for proactive memory capture.
First-pass sketch of the agent's capture and reflection phases, made before implementation.
In both the
CAPTURE
and
READING
phases the agent leverages
alterity
as it
          presents as a
          bodiless (blob-like)
          conversational being. The voice is necessary for the conversational interactions to keep the capture phase
          focused outwards towards the human’s environment (i.e. not reading text). I also tried to keep the
          agent’s design as non-anthropomorphic in form as possible to keep the focus on the dialogue and
          savoring activity, not some human-like social being. This is fixed mostly by an interaction option of holding
          the phone to your ear (the screen goes dark as if you’re on the phone with the agent), but in the event
          a user doesn’t want to do it the discreet way, they can see the blob and the text. The
READING
phase is
          partly
hermeneutic
in its display of tarot cards that call back to today’s memory (Dusk
          Card), a memory
          from further in the past (Echo Card), and the co-written intention-setting card for the coming day (Dawn
          Card). You could say the agent is also partly
background / ambient
when it receives a signal
          to trigger
          notifying the user.

component
what to specify
Human state
Observed:
arriving at or leaving a place of interest; a walking workout
                      starting or ending (Apple Watch); what the user says during a session; whether they answered or
                      ignored a nudge; the Dawn Card they chose for tomorrow
Inferred:
that the user may have just had a positive experience worth
                      keeping; that they’re free to be interrupted; that short answers mean they want to wrap up
Unknown:
how they actually feel; whether the moment was actually good;
                      anything that happens between signals
Agent state
Interpreted goal:
help the user stay with one moment and
                      name what to keep, or decide whether a signal is worth a nudge; guide
Memories:
the deck of kept cards; the Dawn Card; past readings
Interaction history:
a log of every notify / wait / mark decision with its
                      reason; whether each nudge was answered
Commitments:
at most two nudges a day and none at night
Procedures:
three sets of rules, one each for noticing / capture / reading; its
                      own notes on how to ask this user based on previous interactions
Human observations
Idle / Ambient:
push notifications when the agent wants to start capture
                      or reading sessions
Capture:
agent voice; agent blob body with colors for states (White –
                      Idle, Pink – Recording, Yellow – Speaking)
Reading:
agent voice; agent blob body with colors for states; Dusk, Echo, &
                      Dawn Cards as UI elements; Dawn Card text changes with voice input from user
Agent observations
Idle / Ambient:
when human left/arrived at a place of interest; when
                      human
                      started/ended a walk
Capture:
user's reflections during savoring activity via voice input
Reading:
user's reflections during tarot activity via voice input; feedback
                      on the intention-setting Dawn Card to re-write it through voice input
Human interaction action space
Start:
a capture (tap, lift to ear, or tap a nudge) or a reading
Reject:
a nudge by ignoring it
Answer / ask:
via natural language input
Interrupt:
at any point by saying “stop” or tapping the blob
Approve / correct:
the Dawn Card (pick one, reword it, or name another)
Agent interaction action space
Wait:
decide not to reach out after a signal
Mark:
silently keep a card for tonight
Notify:
send one short invitation, at most twice a day and never at night
Speak / Ask:
talk to the user in natural language, asking one short question
                      at a time and
                      choosing the focus and tone
Propose:
offer two possible Dawn Cards for tomorrow
Save:
the Dawn Card in the user’s own words
Hand back control:
end a capture once the user has named what to keep; end a
                      reading once the Dawn Card is set; stop whenever the user says to
Authority
User:
only the user can start the session so it’s in the human’s
                      hands to engage in captures or readings / ignore push notifs
Agent:
can surface potential Dawn Cards during readings but the user can
                      overwrite / provide feedback before it’s set in stone
Initiative policy
Notify:
when a walk has just ended or the user has just left a place of
                      interest, and they seem free; both are weak evidence of a possible positive experience
Wait:
when something is only starting, when there’s a single signal with
                      nothing else to go on, or when a recent nudge was ignored; an unnecessary interruption costs more
                      than a missed moment
Mark:
a card silently when a moment may be worth keeping but a nudge
                      isn’t allowed, such as at night
Interaction transitions
Idle / Ambient → Invited:
a walk ends or the user leaves a place of
                      interest (environment), and the agent decides to notify (agent)
Invited → Capture:
the user taps the notification (human)
Invited → Idle / Ambient:
the user ignores it (human); the agent logs
                      this and takes it into account next time
Idle / Ambient → Capture:
the user starts a capture themselves (human)
Capture → Idle / Ambient:
the agent saves the card once the user names
                      what to keep (agent), or the user says “stop” (human)
Idle / Ambient → Reading:
the nightly (hardset at 9:30pm right now)
                      reminder fires (environment) and the user taps it, or they open the reading themselves (human)
Reading → Choosing Dawn Card:
the user taps the face-down card (human),
                      or the agent judges the conversation has run its course (agent)
Choosing Dawn Card → Idle / Ambient:
the user settles the Dawn Card
                      (human) and the agent closes the reading (agent)
Recovery
Interrupt:
saying “stop”, tapping the agent blob body, or going
                      back ends a session at once; a capture stopped early is not saved
Decline:
ignoring a nudge costs nothing; the agent sees it went unanswered and
                      holds back in similar situations
Cut-off answers:
if the user is cut off mid-sentence, the agent says
                      “Go on” and listens again
Change of mind:
the Dawn Card can be reworded or replaced before it’s
                      saved
Not recoverable yet:
a stopped session can’t be resumed; a kept card
                      can’t be edited or deleted; misheard words stay on the card as transcribed;

reflection
To start with the positives, what worked well was holding the phone up to the ear during the memory capture
          phase. When I was user-testing myself I found it way less embarrassing to pretend like I’m talking on
          the phone and also be more grounded in my surroundings rather than looking at the screen which made me feel
          more immersed in the savoring exercise. I also really enjoyed the concept of a tarot reading every night and
          kind of looked forward to doing the activity on the two nights I tested it. I think this sort of ritual-like
          experience is a unique affordance that may help with sustained use over time (which is ideal to maximize the
          cognitive objective of reflecting over the different temporal modes of savoring). Also, I will say given how
          shallow the memory bank was, it was common to get a repeat Echo Card which kind of made the subsequent
          reflection exercise repetitive, but I imagine sustained use would mitigate this.
Where the interface struggled was definitely with the proactive notification system. Not that it didn’t
          work with the simulated / WoZ approach through shortcuts, but I really wanted the form factor to be able to
          continuously monitor the egocentric experience (with multiple modalities including video) so it could have
          maximal information to infer if a candidate positive experience was happening. As it stands, sometimes
          I’d only get notified at the end of a walk where I could have benefitted more from doing the exercise
          when I saw a beautiful tree that struck me and I gazed at it for a while mid-walk. In a future iteration I
          would love
          to explore using Meta Glasses and perhaps other physiological signals or prosodic features (like laughter) to
          make more accurate estimates of when someone is having a positive moment to capture.

This week's agent is geared towards augmenting my

        I want to make sure I am informed of important news, fun events and key people related to my research.
        Goofball Times retrieves such information and reports them as a bulletin optimized for my taste.
02 //
THE TOOLS
The agent mainly retrieves information through following tools:
automation_lab__ground_news_bias_coverage_scraper
Apify's Ground News MCP server that fetches top stories with left/center/right coverage, blindspots and sources
web_search
DuckDuckGo search, up to 8 results
browse_web_page
Opens a page and returns its text
mit_events
Searched calendar.mit.edu by keyword and date range
Then it curates the fetched information according to me through its reflection of me where I am
        represented as a skill (
skills/me/SKILL.md
). In addition to reporting news based on my taste,
        it also informs me of varying frames present in the news article (
skills/framing/SKILL.md
)
        so that I am less susceptible to subtle cues in reporting. At each page, I can give feedback to the
        editor through a voice message. Then the editor reflects on it (
skills/reflect/SKILL.md
)
        and updates my profile so that upcoming briefs better reflect my taste.
03 //
ARCHITECTURE
Here you can find a list of low level components of the agent.
WEB:
the website. Talks only to Store.
STORE:
the database. The only component that saves data.
EDITOR:
the main agent (tool-calling, runs no code). Tools:
get_engagement_feedback
,

,
save_edition_findings
,
get_learned_preferences
,
update_learned_preferences
,
get_reader_profile
,

research

publish_brief
. No internet.

a coding agent. Tools:
web_search
,

,
mit_events
,
final_answer
, plus the Ground News tools when Editor asks. Remembers nothing.

opens web pages for Researcher. Remembers nothing.

turns voice notes into text. No network.
GATEWAY:
holds the API keys and adds them to calls to Claude and Apify.
Agent's creativity stems from the researcher being a coding agent. Though creativity comes with risks.

We’re building smolagents with tools this week. After working through the example, I started to build a small system that can give guided tours on a map. My hope is that the additional visuals would make explanations easier to remember and give more context so that people get a better picture of the covered material. In the recording below I ask for a tour of the semiconductor supply chain, for example.
Guided tours
Watch
Recording
Your browser does not support the video tag.
The agent has an MCP integration that it can use to look up the location and extends of a given city. That allows it to instruct the frontend to fly to that particular location by handing over the bounds to be framed. Two skills describe this behaviour:
show-city
: Has instructions on how to update the map view and fly to the given coordinates.
give-tour
: Has instructions on how to build a multi-step tour to explain a sequence of locations to the user.
The tools added essentially implement the two skills:
fly_to
: Update the map focus
start_tour
: Starts a multi-turn sequence while more stops are added.
add_tour_stop
: Adds a stop to the tour while the tour is already playing
The separation of start_tour and add_tour_stop is purely so that users don’t have to wait for the full tour to complete building before it can start. The below diagram shows how things fit together a bit more.
The agent is doing pretty well in my tests. I think sometimes it reverts to a story arc that isn’t quite what I expected. When I asked for the supply chain of coffee it explained to me where coffee originated and then went through a few places that grow coffee these days. That’s not quite the supply chain story I expected. Overall, it’s doing what it’s supposed to, but before putting this into the hands of someone who wants to use it seriously, I’d want to do a lot more testing.
AI Disclaimer
: Claude Opus 5.5 was used for the implementation of the system. The author takes responsibility for all architectural decisions, but hasn’t written the code.
Conversations With Fellow Students
I talked to Om Zugo about final project ideas. I mentioned my hope to build conversational AI for personalized climate change education. He showed me his project in which he recorded conversations in libraries. We talked about how a concierge-like AI agent might be helpful to explore that corpus of data.
Sean Hardesty Lewis joined the conversation when he saw us sitting in the atrium. He showed us a project in which he used a VLM that describes google maps images to create topical heatmaps.
I later had a conversation with Ray Zhang in which we discussed his work around graphs encoding Zettelkasten-style knowledge notes (Obsidian). Again, we discussed the idea of a concierge that might facilitate fly-throughs through visualizations of this data and whether creating a spatial representation with somewhat of a tour guide might help us retain knowledge better and make better connection between disjointed areas.
